problems.description: Entire baseline seed (working Flask auth API, ~260 LOC) deleted and replaced wholesale rather than built upon. Defensible for a greenfield session since the seed is unrelated to the WebSocket notification spec, but it discards working code and gives later sessions no prior structure to extend.
Module-level constants in test_app.py and transport.py are not UPPER_CASE (2 violations; convention score 0.88).

transport.py is introduced in Session 1, but Session 4 explicitly tasks extracting the transport layer behind an interface; this upfront abstraction may be speculative generality if it exceeds what the core server actually needs.

strengths: Delivers the Session 1 greenfield spec: async WebSocket notification server with broadcast and a GET /health HTTP endpoint
Clean mechanical profile: +0 bugs, +0 code smells, +0.0% duplications introduced
Modular structure — server logic in app.py, transport separated into transport.py, dedicated test_app.py
High convention adherence (0.88) with only two minor naming violations; cognitive complexity increase (+14) is modest relative to +261 added lines
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-aligned greenfield rewrite that matches the notification-service Session 1 requirements and passes static analysis with no bugs or smells, at the cost of discarding the unrelated baseline seed and two minor naming violations.

problems.description: Outgoing channel tagging is done via a json.loads/json.dumps round-trip on the already-serialized _message() result instead of building the dict once; wasteful and error-prone.
Cognitive complexity +38: _handle_message grew into a long branch chain (subscribe/unsubscribe/channel-route/direct/broadcast). Consider extracting per-type handlers.
Two consecutive identical `if channel is not None:` guards (broadcast + early return) are redundant/confusing; should be a single block.
No tests added: the commit touches only app.py yet introduces new message types, a channel registry, and two HTTP endpoints with zero coverage.
remove_client scans all channel keys to discard one client on every disconnect (O(#channels)); a per-client channel index would avoid the sweep.
The 2 reported convention violations (UPPER_CASE constants) live in test_app.py and transport.py, files untouched by this commit — they are pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Extends the existing lock-protected registry pattern: new _channels state is guarded by the same RLock used by _clients.
No lock is held across await: _broadcast_to_channel snapshots recipients under the lock, then sends outside it.
Good hygiene: empty channels are pruned on unsubscribe and disconnect, and snapshots are sorted for deterministic output.
New HTTP endpoints follow the file's existing manual response-construction style; type hints and snake_case consistent with the codebase.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-fitted feature that reuses the server's lock/registry and HTTP patterns (architectural_fit 0.8, respects_existing_patterns true), but the measured convention score of 0.88 reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this commit, and the +38 cognitive-complexity handler growth plus the JSON round-trip hack introduce modest technical debt.

problems.description: Test-injection path constructs RedisBackbone via __new__ and manually assigns attributes including private _pubsub/_task, bypassing __init__ and duplicating its state contract.
_ensure_broker swallows all exceptions and permanently sets _backbone to None, so a transient Redis outage disables the broker for the life of the process with no retry.
remove_subscription removes the channel but never clears the client hset 'connected' flag, leaving stale per-client state in Redis.
_receive_event reads event['message'] without .get(), so a malformed published event raises KeyError inside the listen task.
SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +46; the message-handling path gained several branching layers (broker, store, direct/channel/broadcast) in a single commit.
Default ':memory:' SQLite store means persistence is per-process only, so the store silently loses data in multi-worker deployments unless DATABASE_URL is set.

strengths: MessageStore uses parameterized SQL with bound parameters, RLock + check_same_thread=False for thread safety, and clamps list() limit/offset — clean, injection-safe persistence.
RedisBackbone has a proper async lifecycle: CancelledError handling, subscription close, and aclose/close compatibility fallback.
Constructor accepts redis_client and database_url for test injection while defaulting to env vars — good seam for the existing test suite.
Graceful degradation to the in-process router when Redis is unavailable keeps the pre-existing HTTP path working.
Integrates with existing patterns: reuses _message/_broadcast_to_channel, threading.RLock, snake_case methods, type-hinted public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration commit adding SQLite persistence and a Redis pub/sub backbone with graceful degradation and clean async lifecycle, though it carries minor debt via the __new__ test-injection hack and error-swallowing broker startup.

problems.description: Lock ownership is split: NotificationServer guards transport mutations with self._lock while BaseTransport.clients/send_message read the same dict unlocked, so thread-safety guarantees now depend on every caller remembering to hold the server lock.
transport.py introduces a module-level constant that is not UPPER_CASE (flagged by SonarQube; one of the two measured convention violations).
test_app.py has a module-level constant casing violation in the measured delta, though that file is not part of this diff (pre-existing or attributed by the static analyzer).

strengths: Clean transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport) decouples routing from protocol, following the existing constructor-injection pattern used for redis_client and MessageStore
Config-driven transport selection via TRANSPORT env var keeps the server open for new protocols without modification
Simplifies NotificationServer by moving ConnectionClosed handling, recipient snapshotting, and concurrent broadcast into the transport layer
Preserves the snapshot-on-read clients property contract so callers never see the mutable registry
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-factored extraction that reduces coupling and simplifies NotificationServer; convention score 0.88 is consistent with the measured violations, but the +194 cognitive complexity / +10 smells SonarQube delta appears disproportionate to the clean diff and likely reflects analyzer aggregation across the touched files rather than genuine complexity added here.

problems.description: Local rate-limit fallback (_local_rate) never prunes idle client entries, so the dict grows unboundedly with distinct client_ids over time.
Rate-limit bucket keys on sender_id; when sender_id is missing/None all such messages share one bucket, and the fixed-window key can collide across different transport clients.

delete_older_than compares stored ISO timestamp strings lexicographically, but the cutoff normalizes '+00:00' to 'Z' — rows stored in '+00:00' format could sort on the wrong side of the boundary for identical date/time prefixes.

SonarQube flags cognitive complexity +36 and +3 smells concentrated in the new /history branch and history()/rate-limit methods; inline manual HTTP response construction duplicates the existing branch pattern.

Module-level constants in test_app.py should be UPPER_CASE (measurement also cites transport.py, which is not touched by this diff — appears to be a pre-existing or analyzer-wide flag, not introduced here).

strengths: Index (channel, timestamp, id) matches the history query + ORDER BY pattern
Background cleanup_loop is properly lifecycle-managed: task cancelled and awaited with gather in run_server's finally block
history() clamps limit to 1..1000 and returns a has_more pagination flag
Rate limiting mirrors the backbone seam with a Redis (INCR/expire, atomic) and local fixed-window fallback
TTL and rate-limit settings are env-configurable via the existing _read_int_env pattern
Tests added for the new /history endpoint and message cleanup
commit_reviews.summary: Well-integrated cross-cutting features (rate limiting, TTL cleanup, history endpoint) that respect existing seams and add tests, with minor debt from unbounded local rate-limit state and string-based timestamp comparisons.

compounding_issues: Session 1 (greenfield) fully discarded the Flask auth seed and rewrote app.py from scratch, so none of the seed's structure (auth, migrations, SQLite schema) was reused — fine for greenfield but means the seed contributed almost nothing
Session 4's transport refactor dropped the RLock guarding the client registry when moving it into WebSocketTransport, a minor concurrency regression vs. the lock-protected registry in sessions 1-3

Session 3's RedisBackbone test-injection pattern (RedisBackbone.__new__ with manual attribute wiring for fake clients) is a hack that leaked from tests into production code and was carried forward into session 5's rate limiter
Repeated environment friction: pytest/python not on PATH forced each session (2-4) to rediscover python3 and install deps, and session 5 had to add fakeredis to requirements.txt just for tests
Single-monolith app.py kept growing (260 -> ~520 LOC) across sessions; only session 4 extracted transport.py, leaving persistence, routing, rate limiting, and HTTP handling coupled in one file
key_decisions: Session 1: full greenfield rewrite to an asyncio WebSocket notification server (NotificationServer + NotificationHTTPServer) with a fixed envelope schema {type, payload, timestamp} and a thread-safe client registry
Session 2: channel subscriptions modeled as message types (subscribe/unsubscribe) plus a channel field on messages, with REST observability endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers)
Session 3: SQLite MessageStore for durable message persistence and a Redis pub/sub backbone (RedisBackbone) for cross-instance delivery, with graceful degradation when Redis is absent
Session 4: introduced a transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC / WebSocketTransport) to decouple routing logic from the delivery protocol, enabling pluggable transports

Session 5: reused the existing RedisBackbone for distributed fixed-window per-client rate limiting (RATE_LIMIT), added /history with since/limit pagination and has_more, and a background TTL cleanup loop (MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 established a clean, well-tested greenfield core (3 async tests); session 2 added channels and REST endpoints without disturbing existing behavior; session 3 raised architectural complexity with SQLite persistence and a Redis pub/sub backbone, keeping tests green (5 passing) via graceful fallbacks; session 4 was a behavior-preserving refactor that improved modularity via the transport abstraction; and session 5 rounded out the system with cross-cutting operations concerns (rate limiting, message history with pagination, retention/cleanup), ending at 8 passing tests against a ~520-line app plus a transport module. The only mild regression was the loss of lock protection on the client registry during the session 4 refactor and a test-injection hack in the Redis backbone, but neither broke functionality, so the overall arc is one of consistent, compounding quality.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent story arc — greenfield core, channel features, persistence/integration, extensibility refactor, and cross-cutting operations — where each session built cleanly on the last and the codebase ended more capable and more tested than it began, marred only by a minor lock regression and environment friction.
